4254:
Added "What-Zit" by L&M Software to Ballyalley.com

This game is very-much like the board game Mastermind-- except you don't need a second player, and the entire game can be played with the hand controller.


Instructions
------------

What-Zit is a fun game using your powers of logic, reason, and deduction.  The object is to guess a number the computer picks, using clues given on the screen.  Two difficulty levels are provided.  Level one allows the computer to choose a 4 digit number with no individual digits greater than 5 or less than 1.  Level two again allows the computer to choose a 4 digit number, with no individual digit greater than 9 or less than 1.

To choose a digit squeeze the trigger when the number you want light up.  Should you wish to keep any digits from a previous guess, squeeze your trigger when the blank square lights up.  After you have entered your fourth number the computer will tell you:

1. How many of the digits are in the right place and are correct.
2. How many of the digits are correct but in the wrong place.
3. How many of the digits are wrong.

Just to make it interesting the computer does all of this but does not tell which number is which.  Anytime you want to quit and find out what the computer's number is, squeeze your trigger when you see the "GIVE" sign.  The number of tries you have made is always displayed in the lower right hand corner of the screen.  At the end of your game, should you wish to play another, squeeze your trigger and a new game will begin.

Additional Notes (by Adam Trionfo):

The blank square that lets you keep any digits from the last guess will place a zero into your guess if you use it on your first guess; zero isn't even a choice the computer can choose from.

The computer can pick the same number more than once.  The most that it replicated a number for me was twice, but when I look at the code, it seems that the number can be replicated up to four times.

If you choose to restart again with the trigger, you begin on the same level as you chose when you first began playing the game (one or two).  If you want to start on the other level, then you must quit the game with HALT and then RUN it again.

Since you have to wait for the moving square to get to the number that you want, this game might have been more user-friendly if the hand controller's knob had been used to choose a number instead of waiting for the square with the number that you want to light up.  This game WAS written in 1981; any program that ran at all was user-friendly!

I played this game one both levels, and it would have been impossible (for me) to beat either level without keeping track on paper of which numbers were in the right place per guess.  If you can remember each guess in your head, then you're a MUCH better player than I am!

You can download the game here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/l&m_software/What-Zit%20(L&M%20Software).zip

Enjoy!

Adam

I've added "Stategic Air Command" to Ballyalley.com (and removed it from the Yahoo message board).  When I typed this game in back in May of 2007 I was having trouble understanding it.  I've included some of the comments that were made between Paul Thacker and myself.

Overall, this program is a simple version of Missile Command.  If loss of lives from attack exceeds 100,000, you lose!  To defend goto TR(1)&(KN(1)

Additional Notes on the Instructions
------------------------------------

Adam Trionfo:  What do the instructions MEAN?  This game is sort of like a SUPER simple Missile Command.  If I press the trigger, then I fire my missiles.  From what I can tell, the knob doesn't do anything and the missiles fire totally at random.  Am I missing something here?

Paul Thacker:  Well, I think you're just about right, but there is some level of strategy to the game. You and the enemy both have a limited number or missiles, which are fired five at a time in random positions. So, depending on how successful your first defense is, you
might or might not decide to fire your missiles again in that round, and risk running out later. Some of the population will inevitably be sacrificed, but you have to try and save as many as you can. It seems to be pretty hard to win, and I gave up after a little while since it's really not all that fun.

Adam Trionfo:
It turns out that these missiles can be controlled... to some extent. While I still can't figure-out what the knob is supposed to do (and neither Mike White or I can find any reference to it in the code), it turns out that pushing left or right on the hand controller will move ALL of the missiles in the direction that is pushed. This isn't really that helpful because if you have some missiles that are going to hit the descending missiles, then you will make those missles miss their target.

The sound is sort of messed up too. There is no explosion when the missiles hit the city (maybe there isn't supposed to be a sound?).

Paul wondered, "It seems to be pretty hard to win."  Well, I ask, IS there a way to beat the game? I guess that if you don't lose over 100,000 of your population and the enemy has no missiles left, then you win. Loosing 99,000 of your population and still winning isn't much of a win though...

I agree with Paul: this game isn't much fun.  Not too fun at all! The game is slow-- which isn't unusual for a BASIC game, but the slowness of the game gets in the way of the "fun-ness" of the game. I will give the game some points for making a pretty convincing cityscape; I like the way that it looks.

4257:
Back in May of 2007 I typed-in several machine language utilities that were published in the Astrocade newsletters.  I wanted to play around with them and then write an article about them for Ballyalley.com.  Well, I DID type in several utilities (seven of them).  I also played around with them.  It was rather neat to watch the expansion of people's perceptions about BASIC transform.  The early newsletters hardly mention machine language at all, but as time progressed, and people tried to take more control of their machine's internal systems, they started walking into the mostly unseen (and unknown) world of the Astrocade's Z80 processor.  I've never seen a history of machine language on the Z80 as seen through the eyes of an Astrocade BASIC programmer.  So, I guess that Ill roll my sleeves up a bit and give it a shot.

I plan to write a short article to go along with the seven utilities before I upload them.  By themselves the machine language utilities would bore most people, but to be able to witness them in the context in which they were first presented would cast a better understanding upon the trials and struggles that confronted those programmers that wanted to write more sophisticated programs using Bally and Astro BASIC.  For those that wanted to squeeze every ounce of energy and power out of the Astrocade's puny 1.8K of available memory-- it meant that they needed to get down to ones and zeros (mostly to be able to communicate with the Astrocades on-board System ROM to utilize built-in subroutines).  Before they could talk in ones and zeros, they needed some tools.  My article will cover some of the tools (both utilities and early tutorials) that were available to readers of the newsletters.  Ill try to write this article over the next couple of weeks, but as I know that time has a habit of slipping away form me give me a tap now and then to remind me.

If you have any general (or specific) ideas that you would like to see covered in an article like this then just give a shout.  Ill see what I can do about plugging away at them too (if they are in context with what Im working toward).

Adam

I said that I was going to make some changes to Ballyalley.com on Fridays.  I even asked for a short list of things to get done (which Paul Thacker promptly produced!)  Well, I wasn't able to get to anything on Friday-- but I was able to take advantage of no classes today (Memorial day) to make a dent in the to-do list.  Heres an overall list of the changes that Ive made to the site.  This is just a birds eye view for you to see what Ive done in the last day and a half.

I cleaned up under the carpet a bit (that is, my hard drive's Astrocade directory).  I was able to weed out a couple of things that had slipped through the cracks.  For instance, yesterday I looked through TONS of backups that I have of Ballyalley.com's program directory.  I used several methods to check to see if I had any doubles, or if I dropped any programs here or there.  It turns out that the 2000 BAUD directory is fine, but that a couple of VERY large 300-BAUD program compilation had somehow been "dropped" from the website.  I'm sure nobody even missed them, as very few people use the 300-BAUD interface, but they are back.

Today I uploaded the few programs that Paul uploaded to the Ballyalley.com FTP site, as well as a few games that I typed in back in May (it feels like I just typed them in yesterday-- but it has been almost four full months!).  I also noticed that "She Loves You" is a program that needs to be looked at (I was glad that I caught that).

I uploaded some interesting games that were written for the PC by Dave Ibach.  These games were originally written for DOS and it takes a bit of work to get them to work (I used DOSBox), but I did have fun getting them going (and playing them a bit-- they're actually quite well done).  I made some screenshots of the games, so if you want to see more about the games, then check the download out as I included the pics with the three Aldo games.

I think that people who have never used the Astrocade will find the videos of the four built-in programs and games interesting.  I'd like to get a few of the more colorful BASIC games on video too, as very few people have seen those.  None of these tapes games can even be emulated, so there are certainly people who would be interested in them.  However, making videos of tapes is a project that's pretty far down the road.  Part of that is because when I reinstalled Windows on my computer recently I have not been able to get the software for the USB VideoXpress (an inexpensive capture "card" that I have)-- I can find the drivers, but not the software.  I may have to order the CD-ROM from the company that makes it.  We'll see.

The math program "The Collatz Conjecture" certainly captured my attention and was much more interesting than I expected it to be.  The opening screen did a good job of capturing my attention.  While it's not a game in any sense, it is still pretty neat to watch.  What I think is really cool about it is just how fast the Astrocade could compute the numbers... well, fast for 1981 when the program was written, anyway (compared to doing it by hand or even calcualtor).  I skimmed through the Wikipedia article that is written about the subject and it's rather neat.  According to it, the "conjecture" still has no proof, but it seems to work.  Maybe I didn't read it carefully enough...

Having all of Mike White's Quadra game all in one place is rather cool.  I'd actually like to follow-up with Mike about this and find out more about the programming about the game.  I find it strange that Mike was such a hacker and programmer with the Astrocade but that he never moved on to the newer systems (unless you count creating tons of Wolfenstein 3D and Doom levels!).

Paul spent quite some time (I think) finally getting a working version of "Michigan Astro-bugs Tape II" going that would work with the menu.  While I think menu systems for tapes are crazy-time-consuming these days, they are still a pretty neat part of the history of the machine.  My first experience with a fast tape was the Coleco Adam (people pick on that machine, yet the idea of the fast tape was pretty good); that system even had a directory.  I remember there was an Atari 8-bit magazine that had a DOS for Atari cassette users.  I also think that someone had hacked the official Atari DOS to work with cassette.  What the purpose of this was, I'm not sure, but it sure puts the historical importance of the tape into perspective.  I guess that European users might have a greater appreciation for these systems-- since they used them for far longer.

Its always good to add a program by L&M software.  Though What-Zit is pretty simple, its well done and is certainly worth a look.  I think that this game was published before any of the tapes were available, so this is sort of a glimpse into the potential of the company.

While Paul Thacker and I have already compared notes on the two darts games that I typed-in last May (and uploaded today), no one else has had the chance to play them.  Both games take a totally different look at the game.  Neither game is my thing, but I dont think that it was a waste of time to type either of these games in (which must be saying something, right?).

I didnt cover all of the updates that Ive made in the last couple of days, for that you can either read through the updates that Ive posted to the user group, or you can read the Whats New section of Ballyalley.com (http://www.ballyalley.com/whats_new.html).

Ill try to get more done this coming weekend (Friday is still the best day for this for me).  The more comments and discussion that I see about what I posted the more encouragement it gives me to post more to Ballyalley.com

Let's see if we can get rid of some of the silence that Paul mentioned!

Adam

4266:
Adam, and The Group;

The story behind Quadra begins in 1983 with the appearance of the
coin-op TRON. I was working at a vending company at the time and was
constantly exposed to new ideas in video games on a professional
level. The "selector" screen in TRON really impressed me, and I
started hatching ideas as to how to employ it to a basic game for the
Bally-Astrovision (at that time) console. I decided since the
evolution of gamimg had gone through three definate steps, I would
feature the best I could of these steps. I had already written a two
player Pong game called Ping (Ping or Pong anyone?), and an Astro
Blaster attempt called U.F.O. Attack (Space Invaders, step two). I
could use Laser Blaster (another previously written program) to
enhance the Pong step, and an Avalanche clone called Landslide (also
previously written) that could play one player only where as Ping
requires two player action. To allow Ping to be a one player game, I
did what the "PRO's" did. I used the one paddle idea in Breakout,
called it Brick Buster, and came up with a "quadrant" that held some
merrit with U.F.O. Attack! (note the colors in U.F.O. Attack, they
were taken from Astro Blaster)!

That left the third step "PACMAN"! There was a pre-cursor to the dot-
gobbler in the coin-op circles called "HEAD-ON". This became the dot
eating half of the third step called Smash-Up. Breaking this step in
two balanced the "Quadrants" and left the maze part for Safe Cracker
which got an idea from "Stranded at Rigel" a program published in the
Arcadian which used a numbers game looking for a combination (similar
to Bagels, also in the Arcadian) then playing a fast moving (for
basic) Space Invaders like game. Safe Cracker is backwards of that.
That is, first you run from the robot, THEN you work the combination
to the safe. Safe Cracker, Smash-UP, Brick Buster, and the menu
driver (which is a super enhansed version of File Searcher) were
written especially for this program. Dave Carson was the one who
called it a "marathon" and asked to be able to play (or practice) the
parts separately. So the "practice" side of the tape was assembled
with the origional Ping, Laser Blaster, Landslide, U.F.O. Attack, and
File Searcher. Two more programs had to be finished up to complete
the set, Smash-Up and Safe Cracker. Dave Carson also gave me a price,
and the AB version was ready to sell.

Tapes were bought from Missionary Tape, and Kansas City tapes. Poly
boxes, labels, and mailers were aquired, and the instructions were
printed. Then the idea of a 300 baud version came up and one was
written, but who's going to wait that long? A "one player only"
version was made, but never sold. Only the "Practice" side of the
tape was used as a demonstrater of 300 baud taping techniques.
(Interesting, but not much fun) Even the "Practice Programs" were way
too slow to file search!!

A few 2000 baud AB tapes were sold however. Then complaints of tape
loading problems started comming in, and THE GAME PLAYER called it
junk, and threatened to trash it in print! So sales went to only a
few collectors. Obviously an Extended Basic version was the only way
to go with this. Two were started. One for a 4K Blue Ram, the other
for 16K, but neither would work as two of the "quadra(nts)"[do you
see whense the name?] used the expander. The project was running into
a brick wall when George Moses learned the secret during his ANNUAL
FISHING TRIP with Jay Fenton! The solution was printed in the
Arcadian! The Extended Basic versions were finished up, the 4K being 
first in three programs. The "selector" and Smash-Up in the first
program, all else but Safe Cracker in the second, and an enhansed
version (of Safe Cracker) in the third. Only one new page of
instructions was needed for the EB tape which also has the 16K
version as well. The "practice Programs" are practically the same as
thier AB counterparts. The 16K version followed the 4K "marathon" on
the tape and included some tape loading enhansements, even a new
program called "The Q Cartoon". Safe Cracker was brought to it's
conclusion as well. This was recieved much better, even Mike Peace 
said it looked good at the "ASTRO-BASH", but sales were impossible
without THE GAME PLAYER's review, and to this day he never bought a
memory expansion!!

When in early 1985 Leroy Flamm made the Blue Ram Utility work out of
a cartridge the entire picture changed. It took another year to put
Quadra with all it's parts into Basicarts (three at first). I believe
George Moses may still have a set of those. That was the 1987
version. It was Ken Lill who suggested the extra man givaway and etc.
This final version came out in 1990, all in one cartridge with
special charactors in the "on board" menu and three switches that
select portions of a 27512 EPROM for instant loading. No instructions
were required other than the ones previously written as no loading
problems or waiting occurs. Henseforth, none were ever made. The
cartridge version was only made from the 16k version, no AB Quadra
ever saw its way onto a ROM. Also, Blue Ram Basic was copied onto the
ROM so as no "cartridge swapping" was needed as was with the first
ones made.

Sorry this was so long winded. Anything I left out?

Mike W.

4278:
I've added sixty-one audio files (in MP3 format) to Ballyalley.com (I've also re-recorded two additional songs).  This is a HUGE amount of music.  Before today there were only TWO songs by George Moses.  I recommend that you try listening to a few of these-- it's SO easy and now you don't need an Astrocade!  George Moses was absolutely the best programmer/musician who got music out of the Astrocade.

Here is the breakdown of what was added:

Bach's Two-Part Inventions (Tape #1) - 15 Songs
27 Christmas Carols (Tape #2) - 27 Songs
Scott Joplin Ragtime Classics (Tape #3) - 14 Songs
Sinfonia to Cantata 29 By Bach (Tape #5) - 1 Song
Miscellaneous Music - 4 new songs, two addtional re-recorded

If you notice the absense of Tape #4, that is because it doesn't have any music on it.  Instead. it contains an Astrocade music making program called "Three-Voice Music Assembler."  This program is archived already, but it doesn't have any music, so in order to use it, you DO need an Astrocade.  I'm not sure if this program is what George Moses used to create his songs or not (anybody know?).

All of these songs were recorded from my Astrocade that has a separate audio-out using a gold-plated cable.  The only way to hear the music better than this is with the original WAV files that I recorded.  These WAV files are much too large to put online, but I do have them safe on my computer and have made a few CDs out of them and listened to them on my stereo: they sound fantastic!

More music to come-- probably on Friday.

Download a few songs and give me some feedback.

Adam

4318:
Well, of course the TRS-80 Model x series had no sound (later models had a
beeper), so sound was generated through clever use of the cassette cable and
an amplifier.  There were actually a few talking games that used this
technique.  Of course an AM radio could be placed next to certain systems
and the interference generated could be used to generate sound as well.  Of
course some systems like the APF Imagination Machine and Atari 8-bit were
able to lay multiple information layers on cassette tapes, which was useful
for a separate audio track, which could consist of anything, even voice.
It's truly wondrous the variety of hacks and techniques used to get
sound/voice out of pre-crash systems.  Again, there's no good reason why the
Astrocade, which is capable of three channel sound output, couldn't use one
of these myriad techniques to generate voice using stock hardware.

 

Again, for pre-crash videogame systems (not computers), the only
software-only speech synthesis I can think of is Quadrun (1983) on the Atari
2600:  <http://www.atariprotos.com/2600/software/quadrun/quadrun.htm>
http://www.atariprotos.com/2600/software/quadrun/quadrun.htm and Spike on
the Vectrex.  The aforementioned Major League Baseball (1980) on the
Intellivision used only that systems excellent sound chip, but it's arguable
how effective a simulation of speech it was.   Spike (1983), while being on
a more powerful system, the Vectrex, I'm pretty sure used software-only
speech.  Relatively low quality and a bit muffled and "fast", but actually
pretty darn good in my opinion and relatively varied.  The details from
Quadrun though probably give the best clue to how to do it on the Astrocade.
Obviously a tremendous amount of compression would be required, but that's
the name of the game with software speech synthesis (look at the fully
narrated second side of the Transformers 5.25" floppy disk for the Commodore
64 from Activision for how far this can be taken, albeit on more flexible
hardware).  

 

Other systems used helper chips within the cartridge, like the ColecoVision,
Atari 2600 and NES, though I don't know if it's technically feasible on the
Astrocade.  Heck, higher capacity cartridges have even allowed the Atari
2600 to run compressed videos.  If there was some way to do a combination of
a bank-switched high capacity (32K - 64K) Astrocade cartridge with a
"helper" chip or two (RAM or sound), I just wonder what could be possible.
I certainly don't know enough of the technical details of the Astrocade to
know what is and isn't possible in this regard though.

Hi,

I had a TRS-80 Model III, and I wrote an assembly language program back in the day that did speech.  Here's the thing though, that was doing recording/playback of speech through the cassette port.  This is easier than speech synthesis like SAM, or the Votrax, because you could only say things that were recorded.

As far as I remember, this technique worked by sampling the "one bit" input from the cassette, and basically reproducing a digital waveform with the same zero-crossings.  (I remember disabling interrupts and cycle counting to get the timing loop correct.)  The quality was pretty bad, but it was understandable.

Somewhere I have the archive with my voice at age 14 or 15... :)

4324:
Adam,

Mostly lurking here.

What Adam is mentioning is the SuperAMS memory card for the TI 99/4A.
The card uses a 74LS612/74HCT612 memory mapper chip. The pages size
from this chip is 4Kb in length. A total of 4096 4K pages, using
12-bits from the data bus, are available. The TI 99/4A has an 8-bit
data bus on the PEB so we have a total of 256 4K pages-1MB total. The
card uses SRAM chips-128K or 512K and that is 1 or 2 128K's OR 1 or 2
512K's. We use mapper registers 2,3 and A-F which correspond to the
lower 8K of expanded memory and the upper 24K of the TMS9900 address
space.

I have seen some fairly large carts made available that used a boat
load of bankswitching.

Adam, and everyone else, I am frustrated by the talk about extra
memory add-ons, and I have talked with Mike White about this. Not that
I am against them-but that Adam here has hit the nail on the
head-Astrocade consoles are dying.

I have been trying to get an FPGA designer to finish the existing VHDL
model that Mike Johnson has done: www.fpgaarcade.com. I am going to
try one more time to get someone then it will be here. I have
dedicated $250 for this project.

It will take the existing VHDL model and modify it to handle the 4 pot
inputs as well. Fortunately, that information is readily available on
www.ballyalley.com.

Mind you, the VHDL model has what we have always wanted.....

HIGH RES!!!

Here is my scope for this:

single FPGA. VHDL core of the Bally/Astrocade
128K SRAM-for video and memory; simple bank switching.
9-bit VGA for 512 total colors.
(composite/s-video out core from the FPGA)
single audio
4 joystick ports including POT inputs as well.
Flash ROM to hanlde multiple cart images.
RS-232 or USB to allow data to be loaded into the PCB.
PS/2 input to allow keypad input

Except for the POT inputs-everything else exists!!!!!!!!!

The VHDL model has been ported to a couple of different FPGA boards so
it can be done-and easily.

James

OK, first my comment about the "floppy disk drive" was incorrect! Since I'm an ex Commodore Vic 20 and C64 owner, the floppy drive I stated was actually used on my C64. Opened the box and we began to use the on board cowboy draw game. The unit died after less than an hour use! I returned the unit and received a new one which lasted maybe a couple hours more. Since I was in the computer mainframe maintenance business I started to look into the problem. Now maybe the information I'm discussing here is old, well known info but I thought I'd pass it along. I opened the Bally case to expose the motherboard and found it covered by a foil shell that encompassed the whole unit. This
 cover was added to meet federal radiation "noise". I removed the covers (I think there was a cover on both sides of the pc board) and discarded. I turned on the Bally without assembly of the outer covers. As I waited for several minutes, I noticed (as I remember it) 2 or 3 chips that began to heat up. One chip got very hot. The heat was, as you know by now, killing the unit. Using a heatsink, I glued it using super glue to the top of each chip. Problem fixed! Let me know if this info is "old"!

The 300 baud format is different from the 2000 baud in that it's
basically just a series of characters, whereas a 2000 baud recording
is more of a binary memory dump.  Of course there are also some
op-codes or something, since there are ways to get 300 baud recordings
to auto-run.

I used the 300 baud interface to save some programs directly to my
computer when I was correcting loading errors in some of the L&M and
W&W games.  You just enter ":PRINT; LIST" and it writes all all the
program code.  There are also ways to write out machine code and such
detailed in the newsletters.

I would love to get some processing tools for the 300 baud recordings,
especially if I try to archive some more of the 300 baud tapes
floating around.  Detailing the format would be a good first step.

Paul

These can be loaded from the computer as WAV files, or made into three convenient CDs for use with a portable CD player. This isn't everything for the Astrocade, not even close, but it is a great sampler by some of the best companies:

Here are some very basic instructions for use (also included as readme.txt):

How to make these zipped WAV files into CDs:
May 2007
By Adam Trionfo

Originally I made these three CDs for Mike White.  They have many of the Astrocade's best 2000-BAUD programs on them.

1) Unzip the three zips to three different directories.

2) Create the audio CDs with a program such as NERO using the WAV files in each directory.  Each WAV file is numbered, so they should be in numerical order already.  If not, then made sure that they are in numerical order before you burn the CD, or else the tracks on the CD won't match the Rich Text file called "CDs 01-03.rtf."

3) Choose the CD track that you want to load with Astrocade BASIC.

4) Loading the Programs on the Astrocade:

4353:
It seems you are describing something like the Kansas City Standard (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Standard ), a tape encoding format used by several computers. I initially thought Astrocade used something like this, too, but it seems data is encoded in a different way in the tape.

Data seems to be grouped in sequences of long pulses, always coming in multiples of four. This excludes the possibility of a conventional binary encoding, as data never comes in a byte-like fashion. If this was the case, there would be mixed amounts of 0es (the short pulses) and 1s (the long ones).

If the pulse sequences are keystroke sequences, my theory is the following:

. Data always comes in groups of four long pulses as some sort of redundancy. If this is the case, the actual keystroke is long pulse count divided by four.

. There seems to be a "random" amount of short pulses between the groups of long pulses. There are two possible explanations:
	they are not random, they are data, and we need to find out how it is encoded, or;
	they are just system overhead, I mean, while the Astrocade fetched each keystroke from memory, it kept generating them for keeping the recording synchronism. In this case, it is not clear whether this is important or not. If we place a very short amount of pulses between keystrokes, maybe the Astrocade will not be able to read data this quickly. If it is not important, limiting them by a safety threshold may improve program loading times significantly.



Ronaldo Goulart


kenn lill escreveu:
> > > When doing serial (300 baud for example) data transfer There are several > things that must happen.
> > 1st, you must set up the timing. this is called the "leader". That is > the long sequence of short pulses.
> Next you need to get a byte of information sent. This has Start bit(s) > followed by 8 bits of information and then youneed to send at least 1 > stop bit.
> The start bit(s) tell the receiver (Bally in his case) that a byte of > information is to follow.
> The next 8 bits (they can either be on or off, depending on whether they > are 1's or 0's
> Then your stop bit(s) tell the receiver that there is no more > information in that byte.
> These bits are sent at a rate of 300 bits per second. Every byte of > saved program is sent to the recording device in this fashion.
> There is a timing circuit in the 300 baud interface that verifies that > it is synchronized with the recorded message coming in.
> Typically, there are 10 to 12 pulses for each byte.
> Finally, there is one last byte of information sent. It is called the > "checksum" byte. It is the total number of bytes of data that were sent > during this one load. This is the way the Bally checks to see if it has > received the right number of bytes. The chance that this number matching > up with the wrong number of bytes sent is astronomical. Finally, there > is a "trailer" burst sent. This tells the receiver that there is no more > data in this load. In 2000 bd, everything works the same, except faster.
> I hope this helps.
> Ken

I opened the 10 PRINT "HELLO" program to examine it and noticed the differences you talked about. They don't interfere in the waveform analysis at all. The only tips I can give to improve the files (maybe useful in case of playback with a sound card with poor amplification) are to use sound editing tools for scanning the offset of the recording and fix it, so it will be centered (in GoldWave, effect-> offset -> scan offset); and to maximize it, so the wave amplitude occupies the maximum possible range (again, in GoldWave, effect -> volume -> maximize). This last adjustment is equivalent to increase the recording volume, but the software takes care to increase it only to a level where the highest wave crests are not cropped.

Apart from this, the only thing that intrigued me was the fact the "Fox and Hounds" recording presents a typical "sawtooth" waveform - with higher amplitudes in the long pulse sequences - while the "10 PRINT" program presents an almost perfect square waveform. This doesn't matter at the interface point of view, as it probably checks only for the zero-crossing points of the sound, but this possibly reflects electrical differences between the device that generated the "Fox and Hounds" original recording and the interface used for the "10 PRINT".


Ronaldo Goulart

4372:
Paul, and Group;

To send to tape the way the "pros" did it at 300 baud, try:

10NT=1;;PRINT ;FOR A=0TO 127;TV=A;NEXT A;:RETURN

And notice the faster "dumping time"! :RETURN does NOT turn off the
300 baud interface in any way, it resets the screen interrupt to
disable the "LITE PEN" interrupt and etc. returning the operation of
BALLY BASIC, HOT ROD BASIC, VIPERSOFT BASIC, or BLUE RAM BASIC to
normal! Only ASTRO BASIC doesn't have this feature. As to COLOR
BASIC, it's mentioned in Arcadian Vol.3 pg.2 which is BEFORE the
development of 2000 baud taping I believe. Henseforth, I would bet on
the 300 baud access to it, not 2000! The :LIST and :INPUT commands
use the "LITE PEN" interrupt to load data and process data in the
same way as keypad inputs. Try saving the above line with:

:PRINT ;LIST

Then hit RESET and reload with:

:INPUT ;FOR A=-24576TO -24547;%(A)=KP;NEXT A;%(-24576)=10

Notice I didn't put this into a line no. Read the Basic handbook on
the use of the "KP" command (any Basic). If I counted right, you 
should be able to use LIST and view your program. You can try it
without that last command, because it's been a while since I messed
with 300 baud taping, and I don't remember how this handles line
numbers. Oh well, the point being that :INPUT (or :LIST) in 300
baud "SIMULATES" keypad input through the "LITE PEN" port which
allowed some of the early users (hackers) to install a full blown
keyboard through this port with a UART of some kind. See the early
Arcadian and or Cursor issues.


And as to the "check sum" byte at 2000 baud, there is exactly a 1 in
256 chance of matching the count with a bad load. Not great odds, but
in theory it CAN happen.

Mike W.

The best way to do this is to do it in a program so you don't have the possibility of needing to retype because of typos

10 : PRINT ;PRINT "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
20 A=KP; :LIST

1) First, after typing in the program, set up your tape recorder to record, but put it on pause.
2) When ready, start your recording , allowing a couple of seconds to clear ony leader tape.
3) Then type in RUN GO
4) When the cursor returns, stop your recorder.
5) Then rewind your recorder to the beginning of the recording that you just did.
6) Make sure that the volume is up high on your recorder. Then press any key. then start the recorder.
7) If a ? (question mark) appears on the screen, it means that the recording and the program in memory are NOT the same.
8) If the cursor re-appears with no question mark, that means that the program and tape match checksums.
9) If not, you'll need to type in GOTO 20 and retry steps 5 & 6 to check once more. If you still get a ?, try doing it all again

LINE 20 will wait for you to hit any key, then it will verify that the recorded program has a good checksum.

Ken

So, Adam asked me about the state of archiving of commercial tapes,
and I figured it was worth a message board post.  Really, even I'm not
entirely sure how much is left.  Certainly many important programs are
now available on-line, but there are missing programs even from the
major companies.  For example, we're missing Flight Simulator
(Astro-BASIC version) by Mike Peace released by George Moses, Asteroid
ZZap by New Image, and Cosmic Saucer Battle by L&M.  I'm not entirely
sure how to classify the various companies, but let's say a second
tier would have companies/authors like W&W, Tiny Arcade, H.A.R.D., and
Steve Walters.  Here the coverage is quite spotty.  So, there's a lot
left, and it will only get more difficult to find tapes as the
remaining items become more obscure.

I mentioned before the idea of filling out Lance's tape program
database (based off of Mike White's list) with the archival status so

4380:
This is going to be a long reply, be warned...

Oh, I'm really glad the file worked. You asked if I already figured out the encoding procedure: not exactly. I'm going to explain what I did.

As I thought, data is stored, as in almost all tape recording schemes, as a sequence of short and long pulses. So, I made a program to scan the file and find them, then regenerate the same pulse sequences to another file, but using a perfect, regular square wave.

So, how this translates into this very respectable compression rate of 290:1? Well, the original wave files consist of a sequence of very irregular pulses. This is normal, as there are countless factors influencing the wave shape, but the undesirable results are very complex waves, varying immensely in shape and length. As this noise isn't part of the original data, we can suppress it. Then, the filtered resulting wave file has large amounts of repeatable data. Lossless compression, such as the one used in Zip files, looks exactly for this, eliminating most of the redundancy, while keeping a way to restore this redundancy when we decompress the file. In short, I cleaned up the wave, so the very simple resulting file can be better compressed using Zip compression.

This is the result of one of my two initial research approaches. Its goal is to make a convenient way to store wave files directly for 300 baud tape archiving. When I finish it up, I'm going to start working on figuring out how data is binary-encoded in the wave files, then to store it in a binary, editable form (maybe we can call the first approach "microwaves" and the second one "Spartan" - This is Sparta!!!! :) ).

The next step is to make this into a usable conversion tool. Currently, I need to convert the original wave file into a raw file, process it through two programs I wrote, then convert the raw output into a wave file again. Not counting the fact I am still having some trouble processing the other wave files (they are encoded in different sample rates and bit depths). But I believe when it's done it will already be of some use, as it will allow to make a bundle of all 300 baud programs into a single file, like the one available for the 2000 baud programs.

Regarding the problematic recordings, we need to analyze them one by one. 300 baud files seems to be recorded using quadruple redundancy (pulses always coming in multiples of four), so this may allow to restore them with little effort. And we need to examine the nature of the noise in these recordings. For instance, one of the times I was listening this test wave file I generated, I heard a strong "click", possibly due to spurious AC interference at my house. If such a thing occurs during a tape recording, it is possible that the recording will be damaged. This is one of the cases the "quadruple redundancy" will be useful to fix a recording. In case of constant analog noise, there are some alternatives to fix it, depending on the signal to noise ratio. Dropouts (when a damage in the tape makes the wave amplitude to be reduced) can also be fixed if they are not much severe. And in case of a complete loss of the data in a given portion of a recording, when I finish figuring out the encoding format, the size of the damage can be estimated, allowing to "patch it" rewriting the missing code.


Ronaldo Goulart

P.S.: I believe I can reduce the uncompressed wave file for the Fox and Hounds test to 1/4, encoding it at 11025 kHz 8 bit, and, due to the way I generate the file, this will result in no quality loss, but it probably will not further reduce the Zip file size.

I've also modified a few to make them easier to use (these are listed separately in each zip archive). The utilities are:


1) Base Conversion by Ron McCoy
ARCADIAN, 2, no. 10 (September 1980): 88-89.

This program converts from one number system to another. Input is in either binary, decimal, hexadecimal or octal format and then is converted into the three other number systems.  Base Conversion can be downloaded here:

ARCADIAN, 1, no. 5 (March 1979): 36.

This program accepts a two-byte hex number such as $D5FF and converts it to a decimal number that can be input into BASIC.  Convert Hex to Decimal can be downloaded here:

3) 'Game Over' Routine by Tom Wood
ARCADIAN, 1, no. 4 (February 1979): 25.

This very short AstroBASIC machine language routine has been modified from its original Bally BASIC form to displays the words "GAME OVER" from the Bally ROM.  'Game Over' Routine can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/'Game%20Over'%20Routine%20(Tom%20Wood).zip

ARCADIAN, 1, no. 6 (May 1979): 43.

by Ron McCoy

ARCADIAN, 2, no. 10 (September 1980): 88-89.

Notes:

- This program was typed into AstroBASIC on May 9, 2007 by Adam Trionfo.

- The Program "Base Conversion" is exactly as it appears in the Arcadian newsletter except that line 5 has been turned into a comment because it was for use with 300-BAUD Bally BASIC.  For those that are curious, line 5 says, ": RETURN" (this command isn't even available anymore in AstroBASIC).

- Some of the text below expects to be read using a monospaced font, so if it doesn't line up, use a text editor to read this documentation.

Description
-----------

This is a 2000 Baud BASIC program for use with a Bally Astrocade and Astrobasic.

This program converts from one number system to another.  Input is in either binary, decimal, hexadecimal or octal format and then is converted into the three other number systems.


Instructions
------------

'Base Conversion' by Ron McCoy puts it all together.  Now you can have one progam that will convert from any of the numerical systems into the other four, rather than have to use individual programs.  If you start with decimal, the program takes the whole number in one piece and converts it.  If you start with any of the other four, you have to enter each digit; as with Hex - to enter 23AC, enter 2 GO 3 GO A GO C GO and that's it.

Additional Notes (by Adam Trionfo):

This program is limited to 15-bits.  Here are the largest numbers that you can enter into each number system:

Binary - 0111 1111 1111 1111  (the zero can't be entered)
Decimal - 32767
Hexadecimal - 7FFF
Octal -77777

Here is an example program run:

INPUT KNOWN BASE
   B,D,H, OR O

INPUT # 32767              (I chose decimal)

111 1111 1111 1111 BINARY
7FFF HEX
77777 OCTAL

INPUT KNOWN BASE
   B,D,H, OR O

INPUT (W/ LEADING O'S)
4 DIGIT HEX #              (I chose hexadecimal)
W 2
X 3
Y A
Z C

9132 DECIMAL
010 0011 1010 1100 BINARY
23AC HEX
21654 OCTAL

This program could use some cleaning up.  For instance when you enter an incorrect input base the program says, "*INVALID-TRY AGAIN*".  It is great that it catches the error, but then it goes on to convert the numbers anyway-- giving you garbage output.  Overall, this is a solid number conversion program that is as handy on the Astrocade as the scientific calculator is for Windows users that use it for converting between number systems.


Adam Trionfo

Description
-----------

This is a 2000 baud BASIC program for use with a Bally Astrocade and Astrobasic.  This program takes four hex inputs and converts them to a single BASIC decimal number that can be used for inputting data into BASIC.


Instructions
------------

No directions in the Arcadian newsletter are given for this program, but this is how the unmodified program is used:

This program accepts a two-byte hex number such as $D5FF and converts it to a decimal number that can be input into BASIC (in this case $D5FF is -43 decimal).  This program is useful since a POKE command in AstroBASIC inputs two bytes at a time in decimal.  Because of the unusual method that AstroBASIC stores the data, the hex bytes must be reversed on input into this program to get the correct output.  So, $D5FF would be input as $FFD5.  This program only accepts one digit at a time.  Here is an example program run:

HEX #
F
HEX #
F
HEX #
D
HEX #
5

THE DECIMAL # IS:     -43

The modified version works in the same way but it has brief instructions:  Here is a same program run of the modified version:

ENTER HEX PAIR IN REVERSE
ORDER (IE $FF00 = $00FF)
FOR CONVERSION TO BALLY
BASIC DECIMAL EQUIVALENT.
HEX #: $FFD5 = -43
HEX #: $

It is recommended that the modified version of the program be used since
the user saves screen room and is able to fit FAR more conversions on the
screen at once.

For more information about hex to Bally BASIC decimal conversion, see "Game Over," ARCADIAN, 1, no. 4 (February 1979): 25.

This program inputs hexadecimal numbers into memory.  There is no need to swap hexadecimal pairs because the program does it for you.

Instructions
------------

Machine Code Mystery.  We've had very few machine code programs for you, and I believe part of the problem has been the awkward entry of the values.  The following program by Al Rathmell makes the machine do all the work of swapping pairs of hex code, converting them to decimal, and POKEing them into memory slots.

The "Hex Poker" program is a small utility routine that will store hexadecimal Z80 Opcodes into memory one byte at a time.  The starting address is entered in decimal (such as using 20180, the Bally BASIC line buffer starting location - note that it is 20154 in the AstroVision BASIC - rf).  This is identified as variable "B".  As each memory location is listed on the screen by this program, enter a two-digit hex code from the keypad.  After the last byte, key in WORDS RETURN.  To run the machine code routine, enter CALL B where "B" was the starting address...

Additional Notes (by Adam Trionfo):

The memory locations that the instructions give for AstroBASIC don't work well for storing AstroBASIC programs.  While you CAN use ANY area that you want, you risk overwriting that area if you're not careful with the area in memory that you choose.  Try using the stack area: 20258.  In order to get the hang of this program, here is an example program run:

STARTING ADDRESS =  20258
20258 =D5   213
20259 =FF   255
20260 =35    53
20261 =30    48
20262 =18    24
20263 =4C    76
20264 =5C    92
20265 =0C    12
20266 =D1   209
20267 =C9   201
20268 =RETURN
>CALL20258

In the above code, the user only enters the hexadecimal code, the decimal that appears on the screen is output automatically by the program.  After the CALL is made, the example subroutine will either print out the words "GAME OVER" or the word "OVER," depending on which version of the Bally ROM that you have in your machine.  Try entering the above program example, it's easy and will give you a good idea of how to use the program.

To understand what the above code is doing, here is the source code from the "Game Over" subroutine (from ARCADIAN, 1, no. 4 (February 1979): 25.

20258:  D5     PUSH DE     ; Save BASIC Pointer
20259:  FF     RST  38     ; Call Subroutine
20260:  35     DB   53     ; SR no. 52, load regs.
20261:  30     DB   38     ; Horizontal screen position
20262:  18     DB   24     ; Vertical screen position
20263:  4C     DB   114O   ; Color and size
20264:  5C 0C  DW   0C5CH  ; Address of message to display
20266:  D1     POP  DE     ; Restore BASIC pointer
20267:  C9     RET         ; Go back to BASIC

"Hex Poker" is one of the few programs that lets the user enter hexadecimal numbers and not have to worry about swapping hex pairs.  If you are just testing some short routines in BASIC, then I recommend this program; it works quite well.

4390:
'Game Over' Routine
By Tom Wood

ARCADIAN, 1, no. 4 (February 1979): 25.

Notes:

- This program was typed into AstroBASIC on May 9, 2007 by Adam Trionfo.

- The Program "Game Over Routine" is exactly as it appears in the Arcadian newsletter, except that it had to be modified to run under AstroBASIC.  The following changes were made:
     - Line 10 now has the program beginning in the stack area at 20258 instead of 20180 for Bally BASIC.
     - Line 50 now has the address of the most common ROM:  the 3159 instead of the 3164.  Because of
     this change, the program will print the words "GAME OVER" instead of just the word "OVER"

- Some of the text below expects to be read using a monospaced font, so if it doesn't line up, use a text editor to read this documentation.

Description
-----------

This very short machine language routine displays the words "GAME OVER" from the Bally ROM.

Instructions
------------

"GAME OVER" characters were mentioned in [issue] #3 as being available by the command CALL(3164).  This command locks up the keypad and you can't get out except be a RESET.  We now have a more practical way to do it, leaving the keyboard fully operational so that you can continue a game after the words show up.  The following program, developed by Tom Wood, executes a special routine to pull out the 'preprinted' statement.

10 A=20258;B=A;C=80
20 X=-43;GOSUB C
30 X=12341;GOSUB C
40 X=19480;GOSUB C
50 X=3159;GOSUB C
60 X=-13871;GOSUB C
70 CALL(B);STOP
80 %(A)=X;A=A+2;RETURN

[In the above program, lines 10 and 50 have been changed from the original listing so that this program works with the 3159 ROM and with AstroBASIC; you can ignore the next few lines about changing the code in line 50.]

IF your machine does not print the whole phrase, substitute 3159 [the line originally had 3164] in line 50.  This is indicative of at least two variations in Bally software in the field.  That is, the location of certain object codes in the 8K ROM of the Video console are no identical in all machines.

For those interested, the following is a listing of the routine [this has been modified from the original listing to match the updated program for AstroBASIC]:

[This eleven-byte program is stored in decimal area 20258 - 20267 (hexadecimal: $4F22 - $4F2B).]

4F22:  D5     PUSH DE     ; Save BASIC Pointer
4F23:  FF     RST  38     ; Call Subroutine
4F24:  35     DB   53     ; SR no. 52, load regs.
4F25:  30     DB   38     ; Horizontal screen position
4F26:  18     DB   24     ; Vertical screen position
4F27:  4C     DB   114O   ; Color and size
4F28:  57 0C  DW   0C57H  ; Address of message to display
4F2A:  D1     POP  DE     ; Restore BASIC pointer
4F2B:  C9     RET         ; Go back to BASIC

The strange decimal numbers used in the BASIC statements arise due to the idiosyncrasy of 8080/Z80 Microprocessors and the way Bally BASIC handles integers.  Bally BASIC uses 15 bit signed integers and stores data into memory with the least significant 8 bits going into the lowest numbered memory location.  With these two things in mind we can see that machine-level routines must be POKEd into memory 2 bytes at a time, after reversing the bytes and converting to decimal.  As an example, consider the first two bytes of the above routine (D5 and FF).  The order of these two bytes must be reversed, the two bytes considered as one signed integer and converted to decimal.  Thus FFD5 becomes -43 decimal and shows up as line 20 in the BASIC language routine.  Continuing,

3035 = 12341
4C18 = 19480
0C57 = 3159
C9D1 = -13871  (C = 1100 which has the sign bit set)

Additional Notes (by Adam Trionfo):

This very short program is the first example of a machine language program written for the Astrocade in BASIC.  It only display the words "GAME OVER" from the Astrocade ROM, but this program was an important step on the road to using machine language subroutines in BASIC programs.

4391:
Memory Contents - Binary
By Max Manowski

ARCADIAN, 1, no. 6 (May 1979): 43.

Notes:

- Modifications, as listed in the original program listing, are by Brett Bilbrey.

- This program was typed into AstroBASIC on May 7, 2007 by Adam Trionfo.

- The Program "Memory Contents - Binary" is exactly as it appears in the Arcadian newsletter.

- Some of the text below expects to be read using a monospaced font, so if it doesn't line up, use a text editor to read this documentation.

Description
-----------

This program takes a decical number as memory location for input, then prints out the input number, followed by the contents of the memory location in AstroBASIC decical format, then the program prints out the contents of the memory location in binary format (also in AstroBASIC format).  Since AstroBASIC PEEKs at locations two bytes at a time, the binary output will be 16 bits.  Finally, the output will be in hex pair, reverse order (i.e. $FF00 = $00FF).

Instructions
------------

"Memory Dump - Binary" was written by Max Manowsky to yield binary output for a selected memory location.  Brett Bilbrey has modified it to give a full 16 bit answer, and added the comments to go with it.

Line 10 asks for the input for the desired location, the machine prints that location and then the PEEKed decimal number.
Line 20 calls for a conversion from decimal to binary, and displays binary.
Line 30-90 calls the decimal to binary conversion, performs a 'ones compliment' on the number and calls the display routine.
Line 1000 stores the binary number as a binary in @(X).
Lines 2000,2010 provide the display routine for the binary number.

What you will get looks like this arbitrary example:
   The location that I requested is 2049
                        2049          5727          .decimal
                                0001 0110 0101 1111 .binary

Additional Notes (by Adam Trionfo):
Remember that the output is in AstroBASIC format; you must reverse the hex byte pairs for the correct results!  For example if you request the first two bytes of the Astrocade ROM (3159 version), then you will get this output:

      0             (Address Requested)
  -3328             (Decimal Contents of Address Requested)
1111 0011 0000 0000 (Binary Contents of Address Requested)
  F    3    0   0   (Hex Contents of Address Requested)

The actual content of $00-$0F is:

       00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F
       -----------------------------------------------
0000 - 00 F3 AF D3 08 C3 61 0C C3 07 20 1C 3C 1C 20 FF

The returned results from the program give you this

       00 01
       -----
0000 - F3 00

As you can see, the bytes are reversed.  In this example you are reading the memory contents of 01 before the contents of 00.  When you reverse this hex pair, then you see that the results from the program are correct.

As a second example, if you request

      2             (Address Requested)
  -11345            (Decimal Contents of Address Requested)
1101 0011 1010 1111 (Binary Contents of Address Requested)
  D    3    A    F  (Hex Contents of Address Requested)

Again, the bytes are in reverse order.  Just switch them around and you can see the second pair of hex bytes (listed in binary) of the Astrocade ROM.

Do NOT make the mistake of taking a set of eight bits and converting them to a hex number; you will get the wrong results!  Convert four bits at a time and your results will be correct.


Adam Trionfo

- Some of the text below expects to be read using a monospaced font, so if it doesn't line up, use a text editor to read this documentation.

Description
-----------

This program takes a decimal beginning memory address and an decimal ending memory address and then prints out the hex pairs.  The output is NOT in AstroBASIC format- the hex pairs are in the correct order.

Instructions
------------

Memory Dump program by Gary Moser prints its answers in hexadecimal language.  See what you get for the location 0006.  If it is 61, then your machine is like mine [Bob Fabris], and it is 66, it is like Tom Wood's.  If something else, then we have more variants on the street.

This program will display memory locations in hex (up to eighteen bytes pairs per screen).  This is most useful for viewing the Astrocade ROM (that was this program's intended purpose), but you can print out any memory location.  Here is an example of a program run of the modified version of "Memory Dump - Hex" (this example is run on an Astrocade machine with the '3159' ROM):

DECIMAL MEMORY LOCATION
STARTING ADDRESS? 0
ENDING ADDRESS? 16
0/00 F3
2/AF D3
4/08 C3
6/61 0C
8/C3 07
10/20 1C
12/3C 1C
14/20 FF
16/C3 0A
DECIMAL MEMORY LOCATION
STARTING ADDRESS?

> AGAIN
YOU KICK ADAM IN THE RIBS.  HE LETS OUT A LOW GROAN.
> AGAIN

Paul wrote:
>>
I'd never even heard of Blitz3D before you mentioned it. It looks like it's most commonly used for game programming.
>>

Yes, that's what it's for: games.  I was also surprised to hear that it was being used for the 300-Baud conversion program.  The Blitz language is most popular in the U.K. (well, so I thought until now).  I can't speak for the PC version, but Blitz BASIC on the Amiga was used because it made programming much easier and you could still get some pretty good (i.e. FAST) games out of it (there are some CD games for the Amiga CD32 that were written in the language, as well as tons of PD and shareware titles for the regular Amiga).  Unlike other BASICs, in which many of the games sort of had the same sort of look, the programmer was rather free to do whatever they wanted to do, so games looked pretty good and different from each other.  I did know that it could also be used for other tasks besides games, but the Amiga was pretty-much a games machine (not counting the video editing that was also done on it), so games was what the language was used for.  Sure, some folks (like me) also used the Amiga for other everyday-type task (Word Processing, Internet, or DTP), but we were certainly in the minority (especially in the U.S.).

>>
If you end up making a version in one of the more common (and free) languages like C/C++, Java, Perl, etc., it would be easier for other people to port and modify.
>>

I agree.  The beauty of Blitz is that you can program quick and dirty, and that is quite fun.  The problem is that it does have some weirdness to it (as Ronaldo said, "the Blitz3D compiler has some idiosyncrasies").  While something that is written in C++ will probably continue to compile under new compilers for years to come, the same can not be said for Blitz-- it was, and I think still is, a language in constant flux.  Regardless, it's good to see work being done on the 300-Baud "tapes" regardless of the language.  Who would have expected that the programmer would be from a country where the Astrocade was never sold-- by a programmer who has never owned an Astrocade, and who has never seen an Astrocade "in the flesh," having only seen digital pictures of the thirty-year old little monster!  Help can come from the most unlikeliest of places!

Thanks, Ronaldo!

The television standard used in Brazil is PAL-M (Brazil is the only country which uses it). For black and white transmissions, it is fully compatible with NTSC, but it uses the PAL color encoding schemes to allow automatic tint tunning. Most televisions available nowadays support both PAL-M and NTSC (and sometimes European PAL standards). For the ones without support, there are "transcoders" available, but the only side effect of trying to display NTSC through a PAL-M television without support for it is total absence of color.

Power voltage here is 127v at big cities and 220v at the smaller ones. Using 110v devices in 127v power lines normally gives no problems, apart from SOME MINOR OVERHEATING, but if your device uses an external AC-DC adapter and you are afraid of this, you just need to switch it for a new one.

4461:
As Adam mentioned, some of the files I uploaded some time ago that
he's looking at are scans of hand labeled tapes.  I've basically been
scanning everything I've worked with in archiving.  Some of these are
no doubt interesting for the website, some perhaps not.

The Paula Ibach tapes came from an auction of David Ibach's
sister-in-law.  They probably belonged to David Ibach's brother.  The
most interesting of these is the Frogger/Super Skier tape.  This has a
typed label.  They are essentially Road Toad and Super Slope, but not
as refined a version as what we have on-line.  For one thing, neither
has a real title screen, and you actually have to load them with :RUN.
 Road Toad I got load, and it seems like perhaps an earlier version of
the game--less sound effects, for example.  Super Skier I couldn't get
to load.  The other two tapes are mainly type-in programs, though one
had what may be an earlier version of Buggin' B.C.  I need to look at
these again to see what all I can get off of them.  Are the other
scans needed for the website?  I suppose not.

I also uploaded some cartridge photos Paula made.  I don't have these
carts, and therefore can't make good scans of them.  However, I know
that Greg Thompson ended up with them, so you might ask him.  (Are you
still lurking around here Greg?)  I also need to check up on the
dumping status of his Solar Conquerer prototype.  That's been gone
quite a while now, though in fairness I did also send the dumper some
very obscure hardware and software.

I also scanned all of the tapes I got from David Ibach.  It's still
not clear what all is on some of these, as I don't have a RAM
expansion to test code for the General Video Assembler.  So, these
scans do have some of the few clues we have in their labeling.  Adam
mentioned the General Video Assembler master tape.  There's also a
commercial GVA tape re-used for the mysterious Honey Bear (seems to
have never gotten past a menu, whatever it was).  I thought some of
them might be interesting because they have unpublished programs on
them.  These are probably the only tape scans we'll get for Contest
Entry/Bug Puzzle #2 Solution and Tree, since the programs were
probably only on these tapes!  The Avalanche/Hang Up tape is also
interesting because it has a date on it and a previously unknown
program, Hang Up.  I don't know if this is actually the final version
of Avalanche, since David Ibach may have gotten it early from Steve
Walters, the other half of General Video.

Paul

4498:
>>
also the basic cart with audio input, can it "read" 300 AND 2000 bauds programs?
>>

No.  Just 2000-baud.  Bally BASIC (the cartridge without the built-in mic jack) needs an interface that plugs into the light-pen port and a joystick port.  AstroBASIC (the cartridge with the built-in mic jack) doesn't support this interface.  Also, they both save completely differently.  Bally BASIC dump each character in a program, then reloads each character as if it were being typed in from the keypad.  Astro BASIC does a memory dump.

Adam
